Thanks for the call earlier. We want to lock committed capacity for our internal clinical-summarization feature. A few constraints from our side: peak traffic of ~1,000 rps bursty (sustained 400 rps day), 99th percentile latency target <350ms for single-request inference, and support for very long contexts (users will send up to 60k tokens of historical context + 2k prompt tokens in some workflows).

Current model preference: a 70B open long-context variant (we can share the exact artifact later). Primary asks:
- A recommended reserved capacity configuration (GPU types + count) that meets the latency SLA for 60k context without excessive cost.
- How quantization (Q8 vs Q4) impacts both GPU count and latency headroom.
- Fallback plan: if we need to reduce context to 32k during bursts, how to route with minimal user impact.

I've attached a short workbook with our expected QPS/time-of-day profile and a sample prompt set. Procurement is cc'd and will want a committed-month estimate and any hardware commitments.

Subject: Re: LuminaryTx reserved capacity — long-context memory sizing & quantization contingency

Karthik / Sean / Asha — I ran a model-specific sizing pass. Below are the assumptions and per-GPU estimates. I kept the math explicit so procurement can follow the tradeoffs.

Assumptions (70B long-context variant, Transformer stack, 40 layers as example):
- FP16 model weights baseline: ~140 GB (70B * 2 bytes)
- Quantized sizes: Q8 ~70GB (approx.), Q4 ~35GB (approx.) — actual depends on quant packing and operator support
- KV-cache footprint: roughly 1.2 KB per token per request across layers in our serving engine (this includes keys+values and small overheads). That yields:
  - 32k context -> ~38.4 GB KV cache (32,000 * 1.2 KB)
  - 60k context -> ~72.0 GB KV cache (60,000 * 1.2 KB)

Single-GPU feasibility:
- FP16 (no quant): model ~140GB -> does not fit on a single 80GB GPU; requires model sharding across >=2x80GB GPUs (H100/A100 NVLink) plus KV offload to host or NVME. Latency impact is material; not recommended for latency-sensitive 60k contexts.
- Q8: model ~70GB, so ~fits inside 80GB GPU but leaves minimal headroom when KV cache required. With 60k KV (~72GB) it still exceeds a single 80GB GPU because model+KV > 140GB. So you'd need either 2x80GB (one for model, one mostly for KV) or Q8 + aggressive KV offload.
- Q4: model ~35GB, leaves ~45GB on an 80GB GPU for KV and activations. With careful compilation and NvLink pooling, a 2x80GB H100 cluster with model replicated across both GPUs (read-optimized) and KV distributed can serve 60k contexts at lower latency than multi-way sharded FP16.

Recommended pod shapes (meeting 99p <350ms target under expected burst profile):
- Conservative (no quant): 4 x H100-80GB in model-sharded configuration with NVLink/IB and local NVME KV staging. Headroom: 25% reserved capacity for spikes. Rationale: sharding reduces cross-GPU collectives cost at this context size, but more GPUs required.
- Optimized (Q4): 2 x H100-80GB with Q4 quant for model weights, continuous KV caching on-GPU for hot prefixes, and fallback route to a 32k-context, single-GPU variant during extreme overloads. Headroom: 20% reserved. Rationale: Q4 reduces model footprint enough to keep latency low with fewer GPUs.

Other operational notes:
- We recommend implementing automatic prefix/KV caching for recurring contexts (clinical history templates) to cut effective KV size by up to 30% for many requests.
- Batching: keep micro-batches small (1-4) to meet single-request latency SLO; use continuous batching for asynchronous workloads.
- Quantization caveats: Q4 can introduce small accuracy regressions on edge clinical prompts. Recommend running a quality eval set (we can onboard your prompt set) and tie the rollout to regression thresholds.

Attachment: I exported the detailed math as "model-memory-estimates.csv" (includes per-layer kv multipliers and example GPU mappings).

-Marissa Cole
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
